html:
Mungo Man is the skeleton of a man buried at Lake Mungo in New South Wales, Australia, found by the geologist Jim Bowler in 1974. He lived about 40,000 years ago, which makes him one of the oldest known modern humans in Australia.

He was laid on his back with his hands crossed, and his body was sprinkled with red ochre. That is one of the oldest known uses of ochre in a burial anywhere. Six years earlier Bowler had found Mungo Lady nearby, one of the world's oldest known cremations.

The finds showed that the ancestors of Aboriginal Australians had reached the continent long before most scholars thought, and that they already had careful funeral rites. They sit with finds like Java Man and Homo floresiensis in the story of how people spread through Southeast Asia and beyond.

For decades the remains were kept in Canberra. In 2017 Mungo Man was handed back to the traditional owners, the Paakantyi, Mutthi Mutthi and Ngiyampaa peoples, and returned to the Willandra Lakes.
